# Weekly Book Topics 50Q - week of 20 Sep 2026 (Mon 21 - Sat 26 Sep)

*Auto-generated for UPSC CSE 2027 prep. Feeds the website's Sectional practice flow. Static book-topic set, not current affairs.*

## Week focus

**Basis:** the **Sunday Sweep dated 2026-09-20**, which plans **Sun 20 Sep -> Sat 26 Sep 2026** - the upcoming week after this Sunday run. Sunday is revision-only under the standing Sunday rule, so all new reading falls in **Mon 21 - Sat 26 Sep**, and this set tests those six days.

The week **straddles a block boundary**: **Mon 21 Sep is the last day of F8** and closes it with the item still owed against its brief, the remaining Laxmikanth bodies; **F9 opens Tue 22 Sep**. The Sweep calls this "the widest-angle week since June", and the set is weighted to match - six subjects, none of them a token presence.

| Block | Source | Q | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Polity - Non-Constitutional Bodies** | Laxmikanth **Ch 54-61**: NITI Aayog, NHRC, SHRC, CIC, SIC, CVC, CBI, Lokpal and Lokayuktas | Q1-13 | Monday's full two-hour block and the largest single allocation. The Sweep insists these be read as **one comparative exercise, not eight readings**, so the questions are written to be answerable only from that grid: source of authority, composition, who appoints, tenure, removal, recommendatory or binding. Q3 and Q10 in particular are unanswerable without it. |
| **Economy - the Economic Survey, Volume I** | Tuesday's macro half + Thursday's real-sector half | Q14-21 | Economy stops reading textbooks this week and starts reading the government's own account of itself. The questions therefore test **the apparatus you need to read a Survey** - GDP vs GVA, the deficit family, FRBM, the MPC, CPI vs WPI, the components of reserves - and not any figure from any particular edition. Economy is studied from **NCERT + Vivek Singh, not Mrunal**. |
| **History - the bridge centuries** | TN State Board **Class 11**: Guptas, Harsha, Pallavas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Cholas | Q22-32 | Wednesday's two-hour continuous narrative, picking up exactly where the post-Mauryan page stopped. The Sweep departs from the roadmap here deliberately - the Delhi Sultanate slips to 30 Sep so that the five centuries between the Kushanas and the Ghurids are not left unread. Eleven questions, because Prelims asks the Guptas and the Cholas more often than it asks the Sultanate, and because **Saturday's temple page is built out of this reading**. |
| **Environment - legislation and institutions** | Shankar IAS, the environmental law block | Q33-39 | Thursday's first hour. The six statutes and who enforces them, plus the NGT. Article 252 vs Article 253, the post-2022 Wildlife schedules, the 2023 Forest amendment, and the Schedule I exclusions that make the NGT question a trap rather than a recall item. |
| **International Relations - Pakistan** | Friday, **both hours** | Q40-44 | Held back deliberately from the Neighbourhood First survey on 13 Sep because it is a treaty-and-security file, not a neighbourhood file. Its first appearance in a book-topics set. Treaty, water, the northern boundary, and the trade and connectivity position. |
| **Art and Culture - temples and caves** | Nitin Singhania Part 1, **Ch 1 continued** | Q45-50 | Saturday's two hours. Nagara, Dravida, Vesara and their sub-schools; then the rock-cut tradition from Barabar to the Kailasanatha. Written to consume Wednesday's history page directly - Q50 is the same Rashtrakuta dynasty as Q30, seen from the other side. |

**No repeats, and the one adjacency is declared.** The last six book-topics sets (26 Jul, 02 Aug x2, 09 Aug x2, 11 Aug, 16 Aug, 23 Aug, 30 Aug, 06 Sep, 13 Sep) closed Polity through the **Union** institutions, the **constitutional bodies**, the **State Government** tier and then **local government and the Scheduled Areas** (Laxmikanth Ch 10-53); Vivek Singh through Ch 14 including Inclusive Growth and Subsidies; Spectrum through the British-rule thematics; physical and human Geography; Shankar Ch 3-8; space, nuclear, defence and biotechnology; Ancient through the post-Mauryan kingdoms and the Sangam Age; Art and Culture Ch 1 as far as the **Harappan, Mauryan and post-Mauryan** material; and IR with the US, China, Russia and the whole neighbourhood except one file.

Every block here is a clean advance. **Polity** moves from the constitutional bodies tested on 30 Aug to the **non-constitutional** ones, which have never appeared - and the set exploits the adjacency rather than avoiding it, since the only way to answer Q3 is to know which box each body sits in. **Art and Culture** continues the same chapter from 06 Sep but a different section of it: that set tested Harappan-to-post-Mauryan architecture, this one tests temple styles and caves, with no item in common. **Pakistan**, the **Economic Survey** and the **Gupta-to-Chola bridge** are all entering the corpus for the first time. This is an advance, not a revision round.

**Verification note.** Facts that are date-sensitive, recently amended, or commonly misstated in coaching material were web-checked against primary or authoritative sources before use rather than written from memory:

- **Q4, Q5** - NHRC after the **Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019**: the Chairperson may be a person who has been **Chief Justice of India *or* a Judge of the Supreme Court** (the pre-2019 position was CJI only); **five members**, of whom one is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court and one is or has been Chief Justice of a High Court, and **three** appointed for knowledge of human rights with **at least one woman**; ex-officio members include the Chairpersons of the **NCBC, NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities**, added by the same amendment. The selection committee is headed by the **Prime Minister**, not the Vice-President.
- **Q8** - the **RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** moved the term and salaries of the Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners from the Act to **rules made by the Central Government**, and the 2019 Rules set the term at **three years**. This is the amendment that removed the CIC's parity with the Election Commission, and any pre-2019 note giving "five years or 65" is now wrong.
- **Q10** - CVC tenure verified as **four years or 65 years, whichever is earlier** - not five. Removal is by the President on proved misbehaviour or incapacity **only after a Supreme Court inquiry**.
- **Q13** - Lokpal: **Chairperson + maximum eight members, at least half judicial**, and **not less than fifty per cent** from SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women; selection committee of PM, Speaker, Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, **CJI or a Judge nominated by him**, and **one eminent jurist nominated by the President**. The Prime Minister **is** within jurisdiction, subject to the five subject-matter carve-outs.
- **Q14** - the Economic Survey has **no constitutional or statutory mandate**; it is prepared by the **Economic Division of the Department of Economic Affairs** under the **Chief Economic Adviser**, and has been tabled separately, a day before the Budget, **since 1964**. Article 112 governs the Budget, not the Survey.
- **Q35** - the **Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022** reduced the schedules to **four** - I greatest protection, II lesser protection, III plants, IV CITES specimens - and **omitted the vermin schedule**. Material written before 2022 on the schedules is unusable.
- **Q37** - the **Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023** renamed the 1980 Act the **Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam** and exempted specified forest land **within 100 km of the international border, LoC or LAC** for strategic linear projects, **subject to conditions including compensatory levies** - it did not abolish compensatory afforestation, which is the distractor in the question.
- **Q39** - **NGT Act, 2010, Schedule I** verified against the bare Act as the **seven** enactments listed in the explanation. The **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972**, the **Indian Forest Act, 1927** and the **Forest Rights Act, 2006** are **not** among them.
- **Q41** - the **Indus Waters Treaty** was placed **in abeyance by India in April 2025** following the Pahalgam attack, and that position has been maintained since, with India rejecting the competing findings of the Court of Arbitration. The question is written around the **treaty's own three-tier machinery**, which is static, and the abeyance is stated only as a dated fact in the explanation.
- **Q43** - the **Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement of 2 March 1963** and the cession of approximately **5,180 sq km** of the Shaksgam Valley; **Article 6** of that agreement expressly makes the boundary **provisional** pending settlement of the Kashmir question.
- **Q29** - the **Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram are structural temples of Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha**, not of Narasimhavarman I Mamalla, who is associated with the **monolithic rathas**. Several standard notes conflate the two; the question is built on the distinction and the explanation states it.
- **Q49** - the Ajanta paintings are **not true fresco**. They were executed on a dry prepared surface, a tempera or fresco-secco technique, and the question turns on this.
- **Q26** - **Brahmagupta is a seventh-century figure who post-dates the imperial Guptas**, and **Amarasimha belongs to the court of Chandragupta II, not Harshavardhana**. Both are flagged in the explanation because both are standard traps and one of them has been examined directly in a past paper.

**Nothing in this set is claimed to be a verbatim UPSC PYQ.** The stems follow UPSC's statement-based, pair-matching, how-many-are-correct and single-best-answer patterns, but all fifty are newly written. The locally stored PYQ files in `data/processed/` were checked for overlap on this week's themes, and where a past paper has covered adjacent ground - Nagara shikharas, Lokpal jurisdiction, Gupta-period scholars - this set deliberately approaches the topic from a different angle rather than restating the question. No item depends on a current-affairs hook: the live items the Sweep attaches to this week's reading (the NGT conference, the Gujarat bustard plan, Semicon 2.0, the Shaksgam Joint Commission, the PLFS August bulletin) are kept **out of the stems** and appear, where at all, only as context in an explanation.

## How to use

**One sitting, 60 minutes, timed, no notes.** Mark and move; do not linger on a statement you cannot place. Unlike the last two weeks this is **not** a cold pre-read diagnostic - Monday's Polity block is the only reading you will not have done when you sit it, and even that is a single day out. Treat it as a test of the week, and re-take it blind on **Saturday 26 Sep** once all six days are closed. The gap between the two scores is the honest measure of the week.

Then debrief in two categories only: **wrong answers** and **lucky guesses**, one line each on *why the wrong statement is wrong* rather than which option was right. In this set the traps are overwhelmingly of one kind - **a provision that belongs to one body or statute being attributed to its neighbour**. CVC four years against CIC three; appointment by the Governor but removal by the President; Article 252 for the Water Act against Article 253 for the Air Act; the Wildlife Act sitting outside the NGT's Schedule I; Narasimhavarman I against Narasimhavarman II. That is exactly the confusion a single comparative grid fixes and no amount of re-reading does, which is why the Sweep asks for Monday's page to be built as **one physical spread** rather than eight.

**Benchmark.** The Easy set (15 Q) should be near-perfect. More than three dropped there means the chapter has not set, and the fix is to re-read it the same evening rather than to do more questions. Difficulty mix is **15 Easy / 25 Moderate / 10 Hard**. Come back for a blind re-take the following Sunday, and keep this file for the **quarterly full GS mock due at the start of October** - Q1-13 and Q33-39 are the two blocks most likely to reappear there in some form.

### Polity - Non-Constitutional Bodies (Laxmikanth Ch 54-61)


**Q1.** With reference to the NITI Aayog, consider the following statements:
1. It was established by an Act of Parliament in 2015.
2. It replaced the Planning Commission, which was itself created by a resolution of the Union Cabinet in 1950.
3. The Prime Minister is its ex-officio Chairperson.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

- (a) 1 and 2 only
- (b) 2 and 3 only
- (c) 1 and 3 only
- (d) 1, 2 and 3


**Q2.** With reference to the composition of the NITI Aayog, consider the following statements:
1. Its Governing Council comprises the Chief Ministers of all the States and the Lieutenant Governors of the Union Territories.
2. Its Chief Executive Officer is appointed by the Prime Minister for a fixed tenure and holds the rank of Secretary to the Government of India.
3. Regional Councils are permanent bodies constituted for each of the six zonal regions of the country.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

- (a) 1 and 2 only
- (b) 2 and 3 only
- (c) 1 and 3 only
- (d) 1, 2 and 3


**Q3.** Consider the following pairs (Body : Source of its authority):
1. National Commission for Backward Classes : the Constitution
2. Central Vigilance Commission : an executive resolution currently in force
3. Central Bureau of Investigation : the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946
4. Lokpal : the Constitution
How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?

- (a) Only one
- (b) Only two
- (c) Only three
- (d) All four


**Q4.** Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 as amended in 2019, who is eligible to be appointed Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission?

**Q5.** With reference to the membership of the National Human Rights Commission as the law now stands, consider the following statements:

Which of the statements given above are correct?

**Q6.** With reference to the powers of the National Human Rights Commission, consider the following statements:

## Answer key with explanations

**Q1. (b) 2 and 3 only** *[Easy - NITI Aayog - source of authority, 1 January 2015 executive resolution]*

Statement 1 is wrong and is the whole point of the question: NITI Aayog was created by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet dated 1 January 2015 - it has no Act and no constitutional provision behind it. Statements 2 and 3 are correct; the Planning Commission (March 1950) was likewise an executive body, and the Prime Minister chairs NITI Aayog ex officio. Remember the ladder: constitutional = named in the Constitution; statutory = created by an Act; executive = created by a resolution. NITI Aayog sits in the third box.

**Q2. (a) 1 and 2 only** *[Moderate - NITI Aayog - Governing Council, CEO, Regional Councils vs Zonal Councils]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: Regional Councils under NITI Aayog are formed to address specific issues and contingencies affecting more than one State or region, they are convened by the Prime Minister, and they are constituted for a specified tenure - they are not permanent bodies, and they are not mapped onto the six zonal councils (which are a separate creation of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, plus the North-Eastern Council). Confusing NITI's Regional Councils with the statutory Zonal Councils is the trap here.

**Q3. (b) Only two** *[Moderate - Constitutional vs statutory vs executive bodies - classification]*

Pairs 1 and 3 are correct. The NCBC became a constitutional body under Article 338B via the 102nd Amendment Act, 2018 (it was statutory before that). The CBI has no Act of its own and draws its police powers from the DSPE Act, 1946. Pair 2 is wrong in its tense: the CVC was created by an executive resolution in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation, but it was given statutory status by the CVC Act, 2003 following the Supreme Court's directions in Vineet Narain (1997) - it is statutory today. Pair 4 is wrong: the Lokpal is statutory, under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.

**Q4. (b) A person who has been the Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court** *[Easy - NHRC - Chairperson eligibility after the 2019 amendment]*

The Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019 widened the eligibility. Before it, only a former Chief Justice of India could chair the NHRC; the amendment added a person who has been a Judge of the Supreme Court. The same amendment reduced the term of the Chairperson and members from five years to three years (the upper age limit of 70 is unchanged) and made the Chairperson of the National Commission for Backward Classes, the National Commission for the Protection of Child Rights and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities ex-officio members.

**Q5. (a) 1, 2 and 3 only** *[Hard - NHRC - full composition, ex-officio members, selection committee]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Post-2019 the Commission has five members - one who is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court, one who is or has been the Chief Justice of a High Court, and three appointed for knowledge of or practical experience in human rights, of whom at least one shall be a woman - plus ex-officio members, namely the Chairpersons of the NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCBC, NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities. Statement 4 is wrong: the selection committee is headed by the Prime Minister, and includes the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the leaders of the Opposition in both Houses and the Union Home Minister.

**Q6. (b) 1 and 3 only** *[Moderate - NHRC - one-year limitation, recommendatory powers, armed forces]*

Statements 1 and 3 are correct - the one-year limitation and the restricted armed-forces jurisdiction (seek a report, then make recommendations on it) are the two standing criticisms of the Commission. Statement 2 is wrong: the NHRC's functions are recommendatory. It cannot punish the violator or award relief on its own force; the concerned government must inform the Commission of the action taken within one month. This recommendatory-not-binding character is shared with the SHRC and, in substance, with the Lokpal's inquiry findings, and is the single most-tested feature of the whole watchdog block.

**Q7. (a) 1 and 3 only** *[Moderate - SHRC - jurisdiction over List II and III, appointment by Governor but removal by President]*

Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The SHRC's jurisdiction is confined to entries in List II and List III, and the Act allows the Centre to entrust a Union Territory's human-rights functions to a State Commission, with Delhi's functions reserved to the NHRC. Statement 2 is wrong and is the classic trap: although the Chairperson and members of an SHRC are appointed by the Governor, they can be removed only by the President - on the same grounds and by the same procedure as for the NHRC, including a Supreme Court inquiry where removal is for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Appointment is State, removal is Union.

**Q8. (b) 1 and 3 only** *[Moderate - CIC - strength, statutory basis, effect of the RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019]*

Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the CIC was constituted in 2005 under the Right to Information Act, 2005 - it is statutory, not executive, even though the Commission was brought into being by a Government notification under that Act. The 2019 amendment is the examinable part: before it, the term was fixed by the Act at five years (or 65 years of age) and the Chief Information Commissioner's salary was pegged to that of the Chief Election Commissioner; the amendment moved both to rules made by the Central Government, and the 2019 Rules set the term at three years. That removal of parity with the Election Commission is what the criticism is about.

**Q9. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - CVC - 1964 resolution, Vineet Narain (1997), CVC Act 2003]*

All three are correct. The CVC was created by an executive resolution in February 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation; the Supreme Court in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) directed that it be given statutory status and supervisory control over the CBI's work under the Prevention of Corruption Act, which Parliament did through the CVC Act, 2003. The Commission was also designated to receive and act on whistle-blower complaints relating to the Central Government, first under the 2004 Public Interest Disclosure resolution and then in the design of the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014.

**Q10. (a) 1, 2 and 4 only** *[Hard - CVC - composition, appointment committee, four-year tenure, removal]*

Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 carries the error: the term is four years or until the age of sixty-five, whichever is earlier - not five. The four-year figure is worth fixing against its neighbours, because this is exactly where mixed-up tenures cost marks: CVC four years or 65; Chief Information Commissioner three years under the 2019 Rules; NHRC Chairperson and members three years or 70; Lokpal Chairperson and members five years or 70; CBI Director a minimum of two years. Note also that the CVC enjoys judge-like security of tenure through the Supreme Court reference, which is why removal in statement 4 is not a simple executive act.

**Q11. (c) Both 1 and 2** *[Easy - CBI - DSPE Act 1946, State consent under Section 6]*

Both are correct. The CBI was set up by a Home Ministry resolution in 1963 but has no Act of its own; its police powers come from the DSPE Act, 1946, and Section 6 of that Act makes State consent a precondition for it to operate in a State. Consent may be general or case-specific, and several States have withdrawn general consent in recent years, which is why the point is examinable. Note also that the CBI has been exempted from the Right to Information Act under Section 24, and that the Supreme Court in the Gauhati High Court appeal has had occasion to examine the Bureau's very legal foundation.

**Q12. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - CBI Director - appointment committee, two-year tenure, CVC superintendence]*

All three are correct. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 amended the DSPE Act to create the three-member committee in statement 1 (replacing the earlier CVC-headed committee). The two-year minimum tenure flows from the Vineet Narain directions, now written into Section 4B of the DSPE Act. The division of superintendence in statement 3 is the one to memorise as a pair: for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act the superintendence is with the CVC; for all other matters it vests in the Central Government. Splitting that sentence in half is a standard Prelims trap.

**Q13. (a) 1, 2 and 3 only** *[Hard - Lokpal - composition, reservation of seats, selection committee, PM carve-outs]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is wrong, and the distinction matters: the Prime Minister is within the Lokpal's jurisdiction, but with carve-outs - no inquiry may be made into allegations against the PM relating to international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy and space, and any such inquiry requires the approval of a full bench with at least two-thirds concurrence and must be held in camera. The selection committee is the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, the CJI or his nominee Judge, and an eminent jurist nominated by the President.

**Q14. (b) 1 and 3 only** *[Easy - Economic Survey - authorship, absence of constitutional mandate, timing]*

Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: Article 112 mandates the Annual Financial Statement - the Budget - not the Survey. The Economic Survey has no constitutional or statutory mandate at all; it is a convention followed since the first Survey of 1950-51. Its recommendations are not binding on the Government, and the Budget presented the next day may depart from them entirely. That non-binding character is the single most examinable fact about the document, and it is precisely why the Survey should be read as an argument rather than as a policy announcement.

**Q15. (a) GDP = GVA + product taxes - product subsidies** *[Moderate - GDP vs GVA, product taxes and subsidies, base year]*

GDP at market prices equals GVA at basic prices plus product taxes minus product subsidies. The practical consequence is what gets asked: because the wedge between the two is the net indirect tax on products, GDP growth can run above GVA growth in a year when net product taxes rise sharply - so a widening GDP-GVA gap tells you something about the tax-and-subsidy position, not about production. Two related distinctions to keep beside this one: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad, and NDP = GDP - consumption of fixed capital (depreciation). The Indian series is currently on the 2011-12 base.

**Q16. (c) Only three** *[Moderate - The deficit family - fiscal, revenue, primary, effective revenue]*

Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Pair 4 contains the standard error: the fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts EXCLUDING borrowings - if you included borrowings the figure would always be zero, which is why the exclusion is the definition rather than a detail. Read the family as a nested set: the fiscal deficit measures the total borrowing requirement; the primary deficit strips out the cost of past borrowing to show the current year's own imbalance; the revenue deficit isolates the part of borrowing that finances consumption; and the effective revenue deficit, introduced in 2011-12, tries to exclude revenue-head grants that actually create assets at the State level.

**Q17. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - FRBM Act 2003, escape clause, N. K. Singh Committee debt anchor]*

All three are correct. The FRBM Act was passed in 2003 and brought into force in July 2004. The escape clause, inserted following the N. K. Singh Committee's recommendations, permits a deviation of up to a specified margin on grounds such as national security, acts of war, national calamity, a collapse of agriculture severely affecting output and incomes, structural reforms with fiscal implications, or a sharp decline in output. The Committee's central design change was to shift the primary target from the deficit to a debt anchor for general government debt, with sub-ceilings for the Centre and the States - a debt rule, with the fiscal deficit as the operational target.

**Q18. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Easy - MPC composition, casting vote, flexible inflation targeting framework]*

All three are correct. The MPC was created by the 2016 amendments to the RBI Act. Its three RBI members are the Governor (ex-officio Chairperson), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy and one officer nominated by the Central Board; the three external members are nominated by the Central Government. Each member has one vote and the Governor has a casting vote in a tie. The target is set under Section 45ZA - currently four per cent Consumer Price Index inflation with a tolerance band of plus or minus two percentage points - and a failure to meet it for three consecutive quarters obliges the RBI to report to the Government.

**Q19. (a) 1 and 2 only** *[Moderate - CPI vs WPI - compiling agencies, coverage, CFPI]*

Pairs 1 and 2 are correct. Pair 3 is wrong: the Consumer Food Price Index is compiled and released by the NSO along with the CPI, not by the RBI - the RBI uses it, it does not produce it. The structural contrast worth carrying into the Survey's price chapter is that the WPI covers only goods at the wholesale stage and excludes services entirely, while the CPI covers goods and services at the retail stage and is the anchor for the inflation target. That is why the two can diverge sharply in the same month without either being wrong, and reading such a divergence requires knowing what each index does not measure.

**Q20. (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4** *[Easy - Foreign exchange reserves - the four components]*

All four are components. Foreign currency assets are much the largest and are the reason headline reserves move with the dollar's value against the euro, pound and yen even when no transaction occurs - a valuation effect, not a flow. The Reserve Tranche Position is India's readily available claim on the IMF arising from its quota subscription paid in reserve assets, and is the smallest of the four. Special Drawing Rights are the IMF's reserve asset, allocated in proportion to quota.

**Q21. (b) The reserve build-up is matched by a corresponding external liability, so adequacy should be judged against short-term debt and the net international investment position** *[Hard - Balance of payments - current vs capital account financing of reserve accretion]*

Option (b). Reserves built out of a current account surplus are earned and carry no matching claim; reserves built out of capital account inflows - particularly short-term debt and deposit schemes - are borrowed, and every dollar of them has a creditor. The accounting identity still balances, so the headline number rises identically in both cases, which is exactly why the headline number alone tells you nothing. The correct adequacy tests are relative: reserves to short-term debt on residual maturity, the import-cover ratio, and the net international investment position, which nets external assets against external liabilities. Option (d) is wrong on a point of definition - the change in reserves is a component of the balance of payments.

**Q22. (b) 319-20 CE, associated with Chandragupta I** *[Easy - Gupta era 319-20 CE and Chandragupta I; the four Indian eras]*

The Gupta era begins in 319-20 CE and is conventionally associated with the accession of Chandragupta I, who took the title Maharajadhiraja and whose matrimonial alliance with the Lichchhavis is commemorated on the king-and-queen type coins. Keep the four eras separate, because Prelims tests them as a set: the Saka era of 78 CE (associated with Kanishka), the Vikrama Samvat of 58 BCE, the Gupta era of 319-20 CE, and the Harsha era of 606 CE. The Saka era is the basis of the Indian national calendar.

**Q23. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - Prayag Prashasti of Harisena - authorship, Ashokan pillar, categories of conquest]*

All three are correct. Harisena, described in the record itself as a high officer of Samudragupta, composed the prashasti in Sanskrit in the champu style, mixing prose and verse, and it was incised on an Ashokan pillar - the reuse of an imperial Mauryan monument is itself part of the political statement. The inscription's classification of conquests is what gets asked: the Aryavarta kings were violently exterminated and their territories annexed, the Dakshinapatha kings were captured and liberated, and beyond them stood frontier kingdoms paying tribute and foreign powers with whom relations were diplomatic. The graded treatment, not the list of names, is the historically significant point.

**Q24. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - Chandragupta II - Western Kshatrapas, Fa-Hien, silver coinage]*

All three are correct, and they are causally linked, which is why they are worth learning together. Chandragupta II, titled Vikramaditya and Sakari, destroyed the Saka Western Kshatrapa power in Malwa, Gujarat and Kathiawar, giving the Guptas access to the western ports and the Arabian Sea trade; he then issued silver coinage for the first time in the dynasty, modelled on the Kshatrapa silver the region already used - a conquest visible in the coinage. Fa-Hien travelled in India during his reign and left an account chiefly concerned with the Buddhist establishment rather than with the court.

**Q25. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - Gupta administration - bhukti-vishaya-grama, land grants, dinara coinage]*

All three are correct. The administrative ladder ran bhukti (province, under an uparika) to vishaya (district, under a vishayapati) to grama (village), with the notable feature that district administration involved local representatives - the town or district council including the guild president, the chief merchant and the chief artisan. The expansion of land grants, transferring revenue and often the right to administer to the grantee, is the change historians read as the beginning of a decentralised order. Gupta gold coins were called dinaras, a term borrowed ultimately from the Roman denarius, and the Gupta issues are the most abundant and artistically accomplished gold coinage of ancient India.

**Q26. (c) Only three** *[Hard - Gupta and post-Gupta scholars - author-work pairs and their traps]*

Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Pair 4 is wrong: the Mudrarakshasa, the political drama about Chanakya and the rise of Chandragupta Maurya, was written by Vishakhadatta. Banabhatta, who belongs to Harsha's court and not to the Gupta age, wrote the Harshacharita and the Kadambari. Two further traps worth pre-empting in this cluster: Amarasimha belongs to the court of Chandragupta II, not of Harshavardhana, and Brahmagupta - author of the Brahmasphutasiddhanta - is a seventh-century figure who post-dates the imperial Guptas, so he is not evidence of Gupta-age science.

**Q27. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Easy - Harshavardhana - Harshacharita, Xuanzang, Kanauj, Prayag assembly]*

All three are correct, and together they give you almost the whole Harsha question-bank. Add two more items: he convened a grand religious assembly at Kanauj in honour of Xuanzang and Mahayana Buddhism, and held the quinquennial distribution of alms at Prayag; and his northward and westward expansion was checked on the Narmada by the Chalukya king Pulakesin II, an event recorded from the other side in the Aihole inscription. That defeat is the hinge of the whole week's reading - it is where the narrative turns from the north to the Deccan and the far south.

**Q28. (b) Ravikirti, a Jain poet at the court of Pulakesin II** *[Moderate - Aihole inscription of Ravikirti, Pulakesin II and Harsha]*

Ravikirti, a Jain poet patronised by Pulakesin II of the Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi), composed the Aihole prashasti in Sanskrit, in which he compares himself to Kalidasa and Bharavi. The inscription records the defeat of Harsha - the only reverse of his career - and is the standard example of an inscription that lets historians date a northern reign from a southern record. It is engraved at the Meguti temple at Aihole. Note the pattern this makes with Q23: a court poet writing a eulogy that doubles as the principal source for the reign, from Harisena for Samudragupta to Ravikirti for Pulakesin II.

**Q29. (c) Both 1 and 2** *[Easy - Pallavas - Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I Mamalla, and the Rajasimha trap]*

Both are correct. Mahendravarman I, also a playwright credited with the Mattavilasa Prahasana, initiated the rock-cut mandapas that open the Pallava architectural sequence. His son Narasimhavarman I Mamalla avenged his father's defeat, took Vatapi and the title Vatapikonda, and gives his name to Mamallapuram, where the monolithic rathas belong to his reign. Keep the next step separate, because it is the standard trap: the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram are structural temples of Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha, a later ruler - not of Mamalla.

**Q30. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - Rashtrakutas - Krishna I and Ellora, tripartite struggle, Amoghavarsha I]*

All three are correct. The Rashtrakutas, founded as an imperial power by Dantidurga, contested Kanauj with the Palas of Bengal and the Gurjara-Pratiharas of western India through the eighth to tenth centuries - a struggle that exhausted all three and left the north open. Krishna I's excavation of Cave 16 at Ellora is the item that Saturday's cave-architecture page consumes directly. Amoghavarsha I, who moved the capital to Manyakheta, patronised Jainism and is associated with the Kavirajamarga in Kannada and the Prashnottara Ratnamalika.

**Q31. (c) All three** *[Easy - Imperial Cholas - Rajaraja I, Rajendra I, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Srivijaya]*

All three are correctly matched. Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur, the largest and most ambitious temple of its time and the fullest statement of the Dravida vimana. His son Rajendra I marched north to the Ganga, took the title Gangaikonda Chola and founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram as his new capital with its own great temple, and sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya in the Malay peninsula and Sumatra - the one major overseas military venture in Indian history, undertaken to protect the trade route to China. The imperial Chola line itself begins earlier, with Vijayalaya's capture of Thanjavur in the mid-ninth century.

**Q32. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Hard - Uttaramerur inscriptions, kudavolai system, ur-sabha-nagaram]*

All three are correct. The Uttaramerur inscriptions, of the reign of Parantaka I, are unusually detailed: they lay down property and educational qualifications for candidature, disqualifications including failure to render accounts, a one-year term, and selection to the variyams or committees by the kudavolai method, in which name-tickets were drawn from a pot by a young boy. Note precisely what this was and was not - a highly restricted, property-qualified system within a monarchy, with no universal franchise and no constitutional guarantee - which is the distinction a Mains answer comparing it with Part IX must make rather than assume.

**Q33. (a) 1 and 2 only** *[Hard - Article 252 vs Article 253 routes for the Water, Air and Environment Protection Acts]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted under Article 253, like the Air Act, as legislation to implement international agreements - specifically the Stockholm Conference decisions - not under Article 249. The contrast between the Water Act and the other two is the examinable point, and it is a Polity question wearing an Environment coat: water is a State subject, so in 1974 Parliament needed State legislatures to pass Article 252 resolutions surrendering the field, whereas by 1981 the Stockholm route under Article 253 allowed Parliament to legislate on a State subject directly, in fulfilment of an international obligation.

**Q34. (b) The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** *[Easy - Environment (Protection) Act 1986 as umbrella law - EIA and CRZ notifications]*

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is the umbrella legislation, enacted in the aftermath of the Bhopal gas tragedy, and its Sections 3, 6 and 25 give the Central Government wide powers to make rules and issue notifications. Both the EIA Notification and the CRZ Notification are issued under it, as are the various waste-management rules - plastic, e-waste, bio-medical, construction and demolition, hazardous and solid waste - covered in the earlier waste block. When a question names a rule or a notification rather than an Act, the parent statute is almost always the EPA 1986.

**Q35. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 - four schedules, CITES alignment]*

All three are correct. The 2022 amendment restructured the schedules from six to four: Schedule I for species given the highest protection, Schedule II for species with a lesser degree of protection, Schedule III for specified plants, and Schedule IV for CITES-listed specimens. The vermin schedule was omitted, and the amendment's central purpose was to bring Indian law into conformity with CITES by providing for a Management Authority and a Scientific Authority. Note that the earlier arrangement of Schedules III and IV for animals, and the separate schedules for hunting categories, no longer exists - so pre-2022 study material on this point is unsafe.

**Q36. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - Protected area categories - National Park, Sanctuary, Conservation Reserve, Community Reserve]*

All three are correct. Conservation Reserves and Community Reserves were added by the 2002 amendment to cover the buffer and corridor lands between established protected areas, the former typically over government land adjoining a park or sanctuary, the latter over private or community land offered voluntarily. The grazing distinction in statement 3 is the reliable way to separate the two older categories at the level Prelims asks: a National Park affords stricter protection, and rights of people living inside are generally extinguished, whereas certain rights and limited grazing may be permitted in a sanctuary. Note also that a National Park may be declared over an area already a sanctuary, but the converse is not so.

**Q37. (a) 1 and 2 only** *[Moderate - Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act 2023 - renaming, border exemption, compensatory afforestation]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: compensatory afforestation and the levies payable into the fund managed under the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 were not abolished - the exemptions granted by the 2023 amendment remain subject to terms and conditions prescribed by the Central Government, including compensatory levies. The amendment's more debated change is its narrowing of the Act's scope, which the criticism argues departs from the wide meaning of 'forest' laid down in T. N. Godavarman Thirumulpad. Read this against the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and the Gram Sabha consent requirement, which is where the conflict actually bites.

**Q38. (a) the National Biodiversity Authority, the State Biodiversity Boards and the Biodiversity Management Committees** *[Easy - Biological Diversity Act 2002 - NBA, SBB, BMC and access-benefit sharing]*

The Act creates the National Biodiversity Authority at Chennai, State Biodiversity Boards, and Biodiversity Management Committees at the level of local bodies, which maintain People's Biodiversity Registers. The functional split is what gets tested: the NBA handles access by foreign citizens, non-resident entities and bodies corporate with non-Indian participation; the SBBs handle access by Indians for commercial use; and the BMCs handle documentation and local-level regulation, with a right to be consulted and to collect fees. The Act's operative purpose is access and benefit sharing, giving effect to the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Nagoya Protocol. It was substantially amended in 2023.

**Q39. (a) 1, 3 and 4 only** *[Hard - NGT Act 2010 - Schedule I enactments and the Wildlife/Forest Rights exclusion]*

Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 contains the classic trap: Schedule I lists seven enactments - the Water Act 1974, the Water Cess Act 1977, the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, the Air Act 1981, the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, the Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 and the Biological Diversity Act 2002. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, the Indian Forest Act, 1927 and the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 are NOT in Schedule I, so matters arising purely under them fall outside the Tribunal's jurisdiction. Note also that the NGT is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure and applies the principles of natural justice, sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.

**Q40. (b) Ravi, Beas and Sutlej** *[Easy - Indus Waters Treaty 1960 - eastern and western rivers]*

The Treaty, signed at Karachi in September 1960 and brokered by the World Bank, gave India unrestricted use of the three eastern rivers - Ravi, Beas and Sutlej - and allocated the three western rivers - Indus, Jhelum and Chenab - to Pakistan, subject to India's limited rights on the western rivers for domestic use, non-consumptive use, agriculture within specified limits, and the generation of hydroelectric power on run-of-the-river schemes. The mnemonic that works is that the eastern rivers are the ones that enter India first and are furthest from Pakistan, and they are the smaller share - roughly twenty per cent of the system's flow.

**Q41. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - IWT dispute machinery - Permanent Indus Commission, Neutral Expert, Court of Arbitration]*

All three are correct: the Treaty establishes a graded, three-tier mechanism - question, difference, dispute - which is meant to be sequential, each stage being reached only if the previous one fails. That sequencing is the heart of India's objection to parallel proceedings, namely that the Neutral Expert track and the Court of Arbitration track cannot properly run simultaneously on the same matter, as happened with the Kishanganga and Ratle hydroelectric projects. Note the current state as a dated fact: India placed the Treaty in abeyance in April 2025 following the Pahalgam attack, and has maintained that position since, while rejecting the competing findings of the Court of Arbitration.

**Q42. (c) All three** *[Moderate - Tashkent 1966, Simla 1972 and bilateralism, Lahore 1999]*

All three are correctly matched. The Simla Agreement is the doctrinally important one: by committing both states to settle their differences by peaceful means through bilateral negotiations or by any other peaceful means mutually agreed upon, it gives India a treaty basis - not merely a preference - for rejecting third-party mediation on Jammu and Kashmir, and it converted the 1949 ceasefire line into the Line of Control with both sides undertaking to respect it without prejudice to their recognised positions. The Lahore Declaration of February 1999, with its memorandum of understanding on nuclear confidence-building, is remembered chiefly for what followed it within months at Kargil.

**Q43. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Hard - Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement 1963 - Shaksgam Valley, Article 6, nemo dat]*

All three are correct. The agreement was signed on 2 March 1963, and the area ceded is generally given as about 5,180 square kilometres. Article 6 of the agreement expressly states that the boundary is provisional pending the resolution of the Kashmir dispute, so the text concedes the very point India presses - that the transferor's title was unsettled. India's second objection is the maxim nemo dat quod non habet, that no one gives what he does not have. Fix the geography with the text: the Shaksgam lies north of the Siachen Glacier across the Karakoram, adjoining Aksai Chin and abutting Xinjiang, with Gilgit-Baltistan, through which the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor runs, to its west.

**Q44. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - MFN withdrawal 2019, Kartarpur Corridor, SAARC paralysis and the BIMSTEC pivot]*

All three are correct. India had granted Pakistan MFN status in 1996 under its WTO obligations; Pakistan never reciprocated, and India withdrew it in February 2019 after the Pulwama attack, raising customs duty on Pakistani goods to two hundred per cent. The Kartarpur Corridor, opened in November 2019, allows visa-free pilgrim access to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib and remains the one functioning channel between the two states. SAARC has held no summit since 2014, and BIMSTEC - which excludes Pakistan and links South Asia to the Bay of Bengal littoral and South-East Asia - has absorbed India's regional effort as a result.

**Q45. (c) All three** *[Easy - Temple vocabulary - garbhagriha, amalaka, gopuram, shikhara vs vimana]*

All three are correctly matched, and this vocabulary answers a large share of temple questions on its own. Add to it: mandapa, the pillared hall before the sanctum; antarala, the vestibule linking the two; ardhamandapa, the entrance porch; kalasha, the pot finial above the amalaka; pradakshina patha, the circumambulatory passage; and panchayatana, the plan in which four subsidiary shrines stand at the corners of a plinth around the main shrine. Note one terminological trap: in Nagara usage shikhara means the whole curvilinear tower, but in Dravida usage the tower is the vimana and shikhara refers only to the crowning element above it.

**Q46. (a) 1, 2 and 3 only** *[Easy - Nagara vs Dravida - distinguishing features]*

Options 1, 2 and 3 are Dravida features. Option 4 - a curvilinear tower crowned by an amalaka - is the defining Nagara feature and is the distractor. The shorthand that survives exam pressure: Nagara temples emphasise the tower and generally lack boundary walls and gateway gates, and are usually built on a raised plinth with a panchayatana plan; Dravida temples enclose the complex within walls whose gopurams grew over the centuries until the gateway came to dwarf the vimana it guarded, and add a tank and subsidiary shrines. Vesara, the Deccan idiom, combines the Dravida plan with a Nagara-influenced elevation.

**Q47. (c) Only three** *[Hard - Nagara sub-schools - Odisha, Solanki, Chandela; and the Hoysala/Vesara distinction]*

Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Pair 4 is wrong: the Hoysala temples at Halebidu, Belur and Somanathapura are classed with the Vesara or Karnata-Dravida idiom of the Deccan, not with Dravida proper, and their signature features are distinct - soapstone as the medium, a stellate star-shaped plan on a raised jagati platform, multiple shrines around a common hall, lathe-turned pillars and unusually dense surface carving. In the Odisha school note the vocabulary shift: the tower is the deul and the hall the jagamohana, the exterior is lavishly carved while the interior is plain, and boundary walls do appear, which is the exception to the general Nagara rule.

**Q48. (d) 1, 2 and 3** *[Moderate - Western Deccan Buddhist caves - chaitya vs vihara, gavaksha, Karle and Bhaja]*

All three are correct. The Western Deccan Buddhist caves - Bhaja, Karle, Bedsa, Nashik, Kanheri, Junnar - were excavated largely between the second century BCE and the second century CE, funded by merchants, guilds and royal patrons along the trade routes from the western ports to the Deccan plateau, which is why they cluster along the Ghat passes. The great chaitya hall at Karle is the largest of the series. Note the functional pairing, because it is what questions turn on: the chaitya is apsidal, has a stupa at its rounded end and is for congregational worship; the vihara is a quadrangular hall with cells cut around it and is for residence.

**Q49. (c) 1 and 3 only** *[Moderate - Ajanta, Ellora and Barabar - religious affiliation, painting technique, Mauryan origins]*

Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is the standard error: the Ajanta paintings are not true fresco - the pigment was applied to a dry, prepared plaster surface, a tempera or fresco-secco technique - and questions exploit this distinction regularly. Ajanta's 29 excavations are exclusively Buddhist and include the celebrated Bodhisattva Padmapani and Vajrapani in Cave 1. Ellora's 34 caves run Buddhist, Hindu and Jain along a single scarp, which is the fact that makes it the standard example of religious coexistence in art. The Barabar caves near Gaya, with their mirror-polished interiors, carry dedicatory inscriptions of Ashoka and Dasharatha to the Ajivikas and are the earliest surviving rock-cut excavations in India.

**Q50. (a) 1 and 2 only** *[Moderate - Ellora Cave 16 Kailasanatha - monolithic top-down excavation, Krishna I, Shaiva affiliation]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct; statement 3 is wrong - the Kailasanatha is a Shaiva temple, conceived as a representation of Mount Kailasa, and it belongs to the Hindu group of the Ellora caves. Its method is what makes it exceptional: rather than being built up from a foundation, it was cut down into the basalt scarp from above, so the entire structure, its gateway, its Nandi pavilion, its free-standing columns and its two-storeyed halls are all one piece of living rock. Note the direct link to Wednesday's history reading - the same Rashtrakuta dynasty that contested Kanauj built this - and the contrast with Elephanta, a Shaiva cave famous for its Trimurti or Sadashiva image.


## Revision checklist

Rebuild only the items you missed. Each line is one recall test, not a summary.

1. **The three-box rule.** Recite it cold: constitutional = named in the Constitution; statutory = created by an Act; executive = created by a resolution. Then place NITI Aayog, NHRC, CIC, CVC, Lokpal, NCBC and the CBI in their boxes - and say why the CBI is the odd one out.
2. **The tenure ladder.** CVC four years or 65. Chief Information Commissioner three years, by rules, since 2019. NHRC Chairperson and members three years or 70, since 2019. Lokpal five years or 70. CBI Director a minimum of two years. Say all five without looking.
3. **Who appoints, who removes.** SHRC members are appointed by the Governor but removed only by the President. The CVC is removed only after a Supreme Court inquiry. Name the three-member committee for the CVC and the three-member committee for the CBI Director, and note that they are not the same committee.
4. **What the CVC actually controls.** Superintendence over the CBI for Prevention of Corruption Act offences only; everything else vests in the Central Government. Half of this sentence is the trap.
5. **The Lokpal's reach over the Prime Minister** - in jurisdiction, with five carve-outs, a full-bench requirement and an in-camera hearing. Not excluded, and not unconditional.
6. **GDP = GVA + product taxes - product subsidies.** Then say what a widening GDP-GVA gap actually tells you, and what it does not.
7. **The deficit family as a nested set.** Fiscal deficit excludes borrowings from receipts. Primary = fiscal minus interest. Effective revenue = revenue minus capital-asset grants. Name the year the effective revenue deficit was introduced.
8. **CPI against WPI.** Which agency, which ministry, which base year, and the one structural difference that explains most divergences - the WPI has no services in it.
9. **The four components of reserves**, in descending order of size, and why the headline number moves on days with no transactions.
10. **Borrowed reserves against earned reserves.** Given a rise in reserves alongside a current account deficit, name the two ratios you would check before calling it resilience.
11. **The four eras** - 58 BCE, 78 CE, 319-20 CE, 606 CE - with the ruler attached to each, and which one underlies the national calendar.
12. **Harisena for Samudragupta, Ravikirti for Pulakesin II.** Two court poets, two prashastis, and the one battle on the Narmada that links the northern story to the southern one.
13. **Narasimhavarman I against Narasimhavarman II.** Rathas to the first, Shore Temple and Kanchipuram Kailasanatha to the second. If you cannot keep these apart, the whole Pallava block is unsafe.
14. **Uttaramerur.** Kudavolai, variyam, ur, sabha, nagaram - and one sentence on what the system did *not* have, which is the sentence a Mains answer lives or dies by.
15. **Article 252 for the Water Act, Article 253 for the Air Act and the EPA.** Say why the route changed between 1974 and 1981.
16. **The post-2022 Wildlife schedules** - four, not six, and what each now holds. Then the four protected-area categories, and which two arrived in 2002.
17. **NGT Schedule I: the seven Acts in, and the three famous Acts out.** Name the three that are out; that is the question.
18. **Indus Waters Treaty.** Three eastern rivers to India, three western to Pakistan, the three-tier machinery in order, and the treaty's status as of this week, with its date.
19. **Shaksgam.** 2 March 1963, about 5,180 sq km, Article 6 making it provisional, and the two-word Latin maxim that carries India's objection. Draw it: north of Siachen, across the Karakoram, next to Aksai Chin.
20. **Nagara against Dravida in four features**, then place the Odisha, Solanki, Chandela and Hoysala schools - and remember that Hoysala is Vesara, not Dravida.
21. **The cave chronology in five stops:** Barabar, the Western Deccan series, Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta. Attach chaitya-vihara, the tempera point, and Cave 16 carved downwards under Krishna I.
